summary:
SphereX Wiki (https://spherex.wiki/) is an ultra-low-latency, open-source citizen science platform designed to discover moving Solar System bodies (near-Earth asteroids, Kuiper Belt objects, Planet X) and ultra-cool brown dwarfs in NASA's all-sky SPHEREx survey.
With over a billion objects observed across multiple epochs, manual review by professional researchers is unfeasible. SPHEREx Blink bridges complex multi-band NASA data and citizen collaboration. Inspired by WiseView, it enables users to blink between observation epochs, compute difference images to cancel static stars and highlight moving objects, and generate deep coadditions to maximize signal-to-noise.
Critically, a single click on any source extracts its calibrated 102-channel spectral energy distribution (0.75–5.0 µm) in milliseconds, automatically detecting diagnostic water ice (3.05 µm) and CO₂ (4.27 µm) signatures while cross-matching in real time with Gaia DR3 and AllWISE. Users can export animated GIFs or publish discoveries directly to an integrated community review forum.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

SPHEREx Blink is an interactive web platform and community discovery engine tailored to NASA's SPHEREx mission. It transforms massive multi-epoch infrared surveys into an intuitive, frictionless tool for citizen scientists and researchers:

- Coordinate-Free Interactive Sky Navigation:
Traditional astronomical tools intimidate users with complex equatorial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) or by having to process the data by themselves. SphereX eliminates this barrier: users can freely pan and drag across the sky with mouse or touchscreen, zoom in and out seamlessly via the mouse scroll wheel, mobile pinch gestures, or preset field-of-view buttons, and double-click / double-tap anywhere to instantly center on any celestial feature. Real-time celestial coordinates auto-calculate under the cursor without requiring the user to type any numbers. For lucky discoveries a random button teleports users directly to well-observed sky patches.

- Multi-Epoch Blinking: Cycles through SPHEREx observation epochs at adjustable speeds (100–1500 ms) to visually spot apparent motion or brightness variations.

- Difference Imaging (Subtraction): Subtracts a reference epoch from each observation frame, removing stationary background stars so moving asteroids, transients, and fast-moving objects pop out immediately.

- Deep Coaddition: Stacks and averages all available epochs to suppress background noise and reveal faint, cold objects otherwise hidden in single frames.

- 1-Click 102-Channel Spectroscopy: With one click on any pixel, our pipeline performs instant aperture photometry across all 102 spectral channels (0.75 to 5.0 µm). It plots calibrated flux in microjanskies (µJy) and automatically evaluates spectral absorption depths for water ice (3.05 µm) and carbon dioxide ice (4.27 µm).

- Multi-Mission Cross-Matching: Dynamically overlays Gaia DR3 optical astrometry (with 25-year projected proper motion vectors) and AllWISE infrared photometry (flagging ultra-cool W1−W2 > 1.2 sources), color-coding candidates instantly.

- Citizen Science Forum & GIF Export: Users can export animated GIFs with a single click or publish candidate findings with persistent spectral data to an integrated community forum, allowing peer review before escalating high-probability discoveries to professional astronomers. click here to see it.

2. The Core Engineering Challenge & Dual-Cloud Architecture

During development, we faced a major roadblock: the official NASA IPAC/IRSA cutout service was heavily congested and timed out frequently (taking 20–45 seconds per cutout or failing with connection drops). Interactive citizen science cannot succeed when users face half-minute delays per image.

To eliminate latency and bypass the bottleneck, we designed a custom Dual-Cloud Architecture:

1. Worker Edge on AWS (`us-east-1`): NASA stores the raw multi-extension FITS files in a public Amazon S3 bucket located in Virginia. We deployed an edge worker in the same AWS region that queries the raw FITS files via HTTP Range Requests. Instead of downloading multi-gigabyte archives, it extracts only the required WCS headers and exact pixel tiles in just 15 milliseconds.

2. High-Performance Core on Oracle Cloud (Ampere A1 ARM64, 24 GB RAM): Located in Europe, this server performs mathematical astrometric reprojection, photometric calibration, and manages a dual-layer caching strategy:

- RAM Cache via Redis: Frequently requested frames are served in 2 milliseconds.

- Local NVMe Storage: Stores pre-processed FITS cutouts and community media.

- FastAPI / Python Backend: Powers the asynchronous REST API and community forum.

This architecture reduced round-trip frame delivery from 30+ seconds to sub-100 ms on both desktop and mobile devices.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

- Democratizing Astronomical Discovery: Bridges the gap between complex NASA FITS files and curious enthusiasts, enabling students and amateur astronomers worldwide to hunt for asteroids and Y-dwarfs without specialized software.

- Pre-Filtering Big Data: Alleviates the burden on professional teams by filtering out noise and false positives through community upvoting and peer review.

- Mobile-First Accessibility: Fully responsive design tested on modern mobile browsers, allowing people to conduct real astronomical research right from their phones.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software

- Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+, zero framework overhead for maximum speed), HTML5 Canvas, Responsive CSS3.

- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, AstroPy, NumPy, SQLite3, Redis Server.

- Cloud & Infrastructure: AWS EC2 (`us-east-1`), Oracle Cloud Ampere A1 (4 vCPU, 24 GB RAM), Cloudflare SSL/CDN, Nginx.

- Astronomical Missions: NASA SPHEREx, NASA AllWISE, ESA Gaia DR3.
